newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: In a first, Guatemala textile union recognized.
newsitem.headline: In a first, Guatemala textile union recognized.

text.p: Workers in Guatemala's only clothing assembly plant with a union Wednesday applauded an announcement that New York shirt-maker Phillips-Van Heusen Corp. would negotiate with the union.
"This means a lot because we have risked everything to fight for a union," sewing machine operator Crisandra Solares told Reuters from the shirt factory.

The move by Van Heusen is unprecedented in a country notorious for sweatshop conditions and labour-law violations in hundreds of assembly plants -- known as "maquilas" in Spanish -- that are owned by U.S. and Korean companies.

Damaris Solis, another machine operator and union member, said Van Heusen Chief Executive Officer Bruce Klatsky visited the Camisas Modernas factory Monday and told the workers they did not have to join the union and also that he had no choice but to negotiate with it.
"We have determined to recognise and negotiate with the union," Klatsky said in a statement Tuesday.
The union is known as STECAMOSA, translated as Union Workers of Camisas Modernas S.A., and has been a legal union since 1991.

Klatsky's announcement was included in a report by Human Rights Watch, which found that while Van Heusen's factories here treat employees well in many respects, they foster an anti-union climate that clashes with Van Heusen's own code of conduct and Guatemalan labour laws.

The report was an embarrassment to Van Heusen, which makes Izod, Gant and Geoffrey Beene brand shirts, because Klatsky serves on the Human Rights Watch board and on President Clinton's "No Sweat" commission, which promotes fair labour practices in offshore factories of U.S. companies.
The 650 workers in Van Heusen's factory earn some of the best wages in Guatemalan maquilas -- from $86 to $260 a month. The factory also has a cafeteria and a doctor on the premises.

But the union complained that Van Heusen broke local laws by refusing to recognise the union since October, when the union said it could legally force negotiations because it had signed up the requisite 25 percent of the factory's workers.
If Van Heusen negotiates a contract with the union, the Camisas Modernas factory will be the only union shop out of 222 assembly plants with total employment of some 54,000 machine operators.

"It would be the only collective bargaining agreement in the maquila sector," Stephen Coats of the U.S./Guatemala Labour Education Project told Reuters. "This is a new way of doing business in the new Guatemala. We hope there's a ripple effect for workers throughout the sector."
Cheap labour in Latin America has attracted thousands of maquila assembly plants, which export mainly to the United States.
The maquila industry began to boom in Guatemala in the 1980s when the government began to offer incentives, including a 10-year tax break, to lure foreign investors.
The Guatemalan government has supported the job-creating maquilas. But many assembly plants have a dark side, including illegal child labour, abuse of workers and back-breaking production demands.

Because of labour violations in maquilas, Guatemala has been under review since 1992 by the United States, which has threatened to eliminate Guatemala's trade benefits under the General System of Preferences, which also includes a yearly quota of duty-free exports to the United States.
